Use the Weave documentation at https://docs.wandb.ai/weave to answer this question:

How do tracing, evaluations, and Signals fit together?

task_plan.description: Explain the roles of tracing, evaluations, and Signals in Weave and how they relate to and fit together with one another.
task_plan.request_quote: How do tracing, evaluations, and Signals fit together?

outcome_assessments.reason: Explains roles and relationships with honest limits.

answer:
Tracing captures what your agent or application does. Signals attach tags and ratings to the agent activity that tracing captures. Evaluations are a separate, dataset-based way to measure an application. The docs I read describe each piece but do not give one combined statement of how all three fit, so the relationships below are my reading of them.

**Tracing is the record.**
- With the Weave SDK for agents, every turn, LLM call, and tool call emits an OpenTelemetry span, which is a structured record of one operation [S8].
- Traces appear in the **Agents** tab. Each conversation shows a multi-turn timeline with nested tool calls, token usage, and feedback [S8].

**Signals are scoring on top of that agent activity.**
- In the Agents view, the Signals tab shows tags and ratings for your agent's conversations [S1].
- A rating is a number from 0.0 to 1.0 assigned to a matching span. Tags are labels on matching spans, such as "user-frustration" or "nsfw" [S4].
- Signals surface quality and safety issues, find patterns, and highlight the traces that need attention [S1].
- Because the Signals tab sits in the Agents view and its tags and ratings attach to spans, tracing is what produces the spans that Signals label. This is an inference. I did not find a sentence that says so directly.

**Evaluations are the structured test.**
- An `Evaluation` combines a dataset of test examples with one or more scoring functions. You run it against a `Model` or a function that holds your application logic [S3].
- Each `.evaluate()` call is an evaluation run. The aim is to measure behavior against repeatable examples, compare changes over time, and identify regressions [S3].

**How they relate**
- Tracing makes the activity visible.
- Evaluations check a version of your application against curated examples you chose.
- Signals score and tag the agent conversations that were actually traced, so you can see where to look.
- Evaluations and Signals both score outputs, but they work on different inputs.

**Limits:** I did not find a passage that says evaluations produce traces or feed Signals. I also did not read the tracing pages on Threads or the agent data model section.

Tracing records what your application does, evaluations measure it against curated test cases, and Signals score and tag agent activity in production. The docs describe each piece separately. The links below are my reading of those descriptions, not a verbatim statement from the docs.

**Tracing is the record of activity.**
- Weave tracing is built on Ops, Calls, Traces and Threads [S2].
- A Trace is the full tree of Calls that share an execution context, and it has a `trace_id` [S5].

**Evaluations are the measured, repeatable check.**
- An `Evaluation` object bundles a dataset of test examples with one or more scoring functions. You run it against a `Model` or a function that holds your application logic [S3].
- Each `.evaluate()` call is an evaluation run, and you inspect the results in the W&B UI [S3].
- The goal is to compare changes over time and catch regressions using consistent examples [S3].

**Signals are scoring and tagging of real agent activity.**
- In the Agents view, the Signals tab shows tags and ratings for your agent's conversations [S1].
- Tags are labels such as "user-frustration" or "nsfw". A rating is a number from 0.0 to 1.0 [S4].
- Signals flag quality and safety problems, help you find patterns, and point you to the traces that need attention [S1].
- Signals can score agent turns with an LLM judge or with an HTTP endpoint that you host [S1].
- The docs say Agent Lens uses the same trace data as Weave, so traces you already send appear there [S1]. Signals therefore work from the activity you have traced.

**How they fit together**
1. Trace your application or agent, so its activity is captured.
2. Use evaluations during development to score a model or function against fixed test examples. This tells you whether a change helped.
3. Use Signals on the traced agent conversations to surface issues as real users interact with it.

Scoring is a common idea across evaluations and Signals, but they apply it to different data. Evaluations score a curated dataset that you define. Signals score the agent turns that tracing has recorded.

**Limits of what I read:** I did not find a page that explicitly ties evaluations to Signals. I also did not read the tracing pages on agent tracing setup or the Threads section.

# Trace your agents

> Use the Weave SDK to instrument multi-turn agentic applications and view them in the Agents tab.

> [!TIP]
>
> **This workflow is also available in CoreWeave Agent Lens.** Agent Lens is the Forge experience built for tracing, monitoring, and analyzing AI agents, with automated insights into agent failures and user intents. It uses the same trace data as Weights & Biases Weave, so the traces you already send appear there with nothing to migrate.
> [See how to do this in Agent Lens](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/agent-lens/tracing/instrument.md).

Learn how to instrument a multi-turn agentic application using the W\&B Weave SDK so that you can view, debug, and evaluate your agent's behavior. This guide is intended for developers who build or integrate agents and want structured visibility into conversations, turns, LLM calls, and tool executions.

The Weave SDK for Agents models the full lifecycle of a multi-turn agent conversation: the agent that owns many conversations, the conversation that groups turns together, each user-agent exchange (turn), the LLM calls within a turn, and the tool executions that an LLM triggers. Traces appear in the **Agents** tab of your Weave project. Each conversation shows a multi-turn timeline with nested tool calls, token usage, and feedback.

Weave is built on [OpenTelemetry (OTel)](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/concepts/), the open standard for distributed tracing. Every turn, LLM call, and tool call emits an OTel *span* (a structured record of one operation). Each span is tagged with [GenAI semantic-convention](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/semconv/gen-ai/) attributes like `gen_ai.agent.name` and `gen_ai.conversation.id`.

If you're tracing individual functions as Ops with the `@weave.op` decorator, see [Trace LLM applications](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/tracking/tracing.md) instead.

# Monitor your agents with signals

> Use Weave signals to score agent turns, apply tags, and surface quality and safety issues in production.

> [!TIP]
>
> **This workflow is also available in CoreWeave Agent Lens.** Agent Lens is the Forge experience built for tracing, monitoring, and analyzing AI agents, with automated insights into agent failures and user intents. It uses the same trace data as Weights & Biases Weave, so the traces you already send appear there with nothing to migrate.
> [See how to do this in Agent Lens](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/agent-lens/tags/create-tag.md).

In Weave's [Agents view](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/tracking/view-agent-activity.md), the Signals tab shows tags and ratings for your agent's conversations. Signals surface quality and safety issues to flag problems, find patterns, and highlight the traces that need your attention. Use signals to automatically score the quality of your agent's responses, notice when a user is frustrated, or flag NSFW content.

To score turns with an HTTP endpoint that you host instead of an LLM judge, see [Score agent turns with a remote scorer](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/tracking/remote-scorer-signals.md).

# Evaluations overview

> Evaluation-driven LLM application development to systematically improve applications

*Evaluation-driven LLM application development* helps you systematically improve LLM applications by measuring their behavior using consistent, curated examples.

This guide shows you how to set up and run evaluations in Weave so you can measure your LLM application's performance against repeatable test cases, compare changes over time, and identify regressions. It's intended for developers building LLM applications who want to move beyond ad hoc testing into a structured, measurable workflow.

**Python**

In Weave, the core of the workflow is the *`Evaluation` object*, which defines:

* A [`Dataset`](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/core-types/datasets) or list of dictionaries for test examples.
* One or more [scoring functions](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/evaluation/scorers.md).
* Optional configuration like [input preprocessing](#format-dataset-rows-before-evaluating).

Once you've defined the `Evaluation`, you can run it against a [`Model`](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/core-types/models) object or any custom function containing LLM application logic. Each call to `.evaluate()` triggers an *evaluation run*. Think of the `Evaluation` object as a blueprint, and each run as a measurement of how your application performs under that setup.

**TypeScript**

In Weave, the core of the workflow is the *`Evaluation` object*, which defines:

* A [`Dataset`](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/core-types/datasets) or array of objects for test examples.
* One or more [scoring functions](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/evaluation/scorers.md).

Once you've defined the `Evaluation`, you can run it against any function wrapped with `weave.op`. Each call to `.evaluate()` triggers an *evaluation run*. Think of the `Evaluation` object as a blueprint, and each run as a measurement of how your application performs under that setup.

> [!NOTE]
>
> The TypeScript SDK uses function-based models and scorers. Class-based `Model` and `Scorer` types are not yet available in TypeScript.

To get started with evaluations, complete the following steps:

1. [Create an `Evaluation` object](#create-an-evaluation-object)
2. [Define a dataset of examples](#define-a-dataset-of-test-examples)
3. [Define scoring functions](#define-scoring-functions)
4. [Define a model or function to evaluate](#define-a-model-or-function-to-evaluate)
5. [Run the evaluation](#run-the-evaluation)

After completing these steps, you'll have a reusable evaluation configuration and an evaluation run whose results you can inspect in the Weights & Biases UI. For a complete evaluation code sample, see the [full evaluation code example](#full-evaluation-code-example). You can also learn more about [advanced evaluation features](#advanced-evaluation-usage) like [Saved views](#saved-views) and [Imperative evaluations](#imperative-evaluations-evaluationlogger).

# Evaluations overview

> Evaluation-driven LLM application development to systematically improve applications

*Evaluation-driven LLM application development* helps you systematically improve LLM applications by measuring their behavior using consistent, curated examples.

This guide shows you how to set up and run evaluations in Weave so you can measure your LLM application's performance against repeatable test cases, compare changes over time, and identify regressions. It's intended for developers building LLM applications who want to move beyond ad hoc testing into a structured, measurable workflow.

**Python**

In Weave, the core of the workflow is the *`Evaluation` object*, which defines:

* A [`Dataset`](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/core-types/datasets) or list of dictionaries for test examples.
* One or more [scoring functions](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/evaluation/scorers.md).
* Optional configuration like [input preprocessing](#format-dataset-rows-before-evaluating).

Once you've defined the `Evaluation`, you can run it against a [`Model`](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/core-types/models) object or any custom function containing LLM application logic. Each call to `.evaluate()` triggers an *evaluation run*. Think of the `Evaluation` object as a blueprint, and each run as a measurement of how your application performs under that setup.

**TypeScript**

In Weave, the core of the workflow is the *`Evaluation` object*, which defines:

* A [`Dataset`](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/core-types/datasets) or array of objects for test examples.
* One or more [scoring functions](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/evaluation/scorers.md).

Once you've defined the `Evaluation`, you can run it against any function wrapped with `weave.op`. Each call to `.evaluate()` triggers an *evaluation run*. Think of the `Evaluation` object as a blueprint, and each run as a measurement of how your application performs under that setup.

> [!NOTE]
>
> The TypeScript SDK uses function-based models and scorers. Class-based `Model` and `Scorer` types are not yet available in TypeScript.

To get started with evaluations, complete the following steps:

1. [Create an `Evaluation` object](#create-an-evaluation-object)
2. [Define a dataset of examples](#define-a-dataset-of-test-examples)
3. [Define scoring functions](#define-scoring-functions)
4. [Define a model or function to evaluate](#define-a-model-or-function-to-evaluate)
5. [Run the evaluation](#run-the-evaluation)

After completing these steps, you'll have a reusable evaluation configuration and an evaluation run whose results you can inspect in the Weights & Biases UI. For a complete evaluation code sample, see the [full evaluation code example](#full-evaluation-code-example). You can also learn more about [advanced evaluation features](#advanced-evaluation-usage) like [Saved views](#saved-views) and [Imperative evaluations](#imperative-evaluations-evaluationlogger).

## Key terms

* **Turn**: One back-and-forth exchange between the user and the agent.
* **Rating**: A numeric score between 0.0 and 1.0 assigned to a matching span.
* **Tags**: Labels assigned to matching spans, such as "user-frustration" or "nsfw".

## Traces

Traces are full trees of Calls that share the same execution context. Each Trace contains an ID (`trace_id`) you can use to retrieve the entire tree of Calls. If you retrieve Call information using the Call's ID, Weave returns data about the specified Call only, and none of its child Calls.

all_read_evidence.heading: How Weave normalizes scores
all_read_evidence.text:
## How Weave normalizes scores

Before Weave stores a signal result, it normalizes the tags, ratings, and reasons that the scorer returned:

* Tags are lowercased. Characters other than `0-9`, `a-z`, `A-Z`, space, and `. , ; - & ! @ # $ % ?` are removed. Runs of whitespace, underscores, and dashes collapse into one dash.
* At most 10 tags are kept per result. Duplicate tags are dropped.
* Reasons have the same characters removed and are truncated to 256 characters.
* A tag longer than 36 characters, or a result with more than one rating, is rejected as a whole, and Weave writes no feedback for it.

These rules apply to every signal, whether an LLM judge or a [remote scorer](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/tracking/remote-scorer-signals.md) produced the result.

# Trace your agents

> Use the Weave SDK to instrument multi-turn agentic applications and view them in the Agents tab.

> [!TIP]
>
> **This workflow is also available in CoreWeave Agent Lens.** Agent Lens is the Forge experience built for tracing, monitoring, and analyzing AI agents, with automated insights into agent failures and user intents. It uses the same trace data as Weights & Biases Weave, so the traces you already send appear there with nothing to migrate.
> [See how to do this in Agent Lens](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/agent-lens/tracing/instrument.md).

Learn how to instrument a multi-turn agentic application using the W\&B Weave SDK so that you can view, debug, and evaluate your agent's behavior. This guide is intended for developers who build or integrate agents and want structured visibility into conversations, turns, LLM calls, and tool executions.

The Weave SDK for Agents models the full lifecycle of a multi-turn agent conversation: the agent that owns many conversations, the conversation that groups turns together, each user-agent exchange (turn), the LLM calls within a turn, and the tool executions that an LLM triggers. Traces appear in the **Agents** tab of your Weave project. Each conversation shows a multi-turn timeline with nested tool calls, token usage, and feedback.

Weave is built on [OpenTelemetry (OTel)](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/concepts/), the open standard for distributed tracing. Every turn, LLM call, and tool call emits an OTel *span* (a structured record of one operation). Each span is tagged with [GenAI semantic-convention](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/semconv/gen-ai/) attributes like `gen_ai.agent.name` and `gen_ai.conversation.id`.

If you're tracing individual functions as Ops with the `@weave.op` decorator, see [Trace LLM applications](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/tracking/tracing.md) instead.

# View agent activity

> Use Weave's Agents view to understand what your agent did, how much it cost, and exactly where things went right or wrong.

> [!TIP]
>
> **This workflow is also available in CoreWeave Agent Lens.** Agent Lens is the Forge experience built for tracing, monitoring, and analyzing AI agents, with automated insights into agent failures and user intents. It uses the same trace data as Weights & Biases Weave, so the traces you already send appear there with nothing to migrate.
> [See how to do this in Agent Lens](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/agent-lens/conversations/view-activity.md).

The Agents view gives you a turn-by-turn record of every conversation your agent had, along with token usage, tool invocations, and execution spans.

Agent applications are hard to debug because the interesting behavior happens between the user's request and the final response. The Agents view in Weave makes that middle layer visible. Every conversation your agent had is captured here, with the full message history, span-level execution detail, and token costs attached. You can see at a glance whether an agent completed its task, how many tool calls it made, and where time or budget was spent. For teams building and iterating on agents, this is the starting point for understanding behavior in production.

## Manage active signals

After your signals are running, you can review which ones are active or turn off signals you no longer need. To view or remove active signals:

1. From the Monitors page, select the **Manage signals** () button. This opens a drawer listing all currently active signals grouped by category.

Removing a signal stops scoring new traces. Weave preserves existing scores from the signal.

results.title: Monitor using built-in signals
results.heading: Available signals
results.snippet:
## Available signals

Weave offers monitors with built-in signals: preset scorers that evaluate production traces for common quality issues and errors by default, with no custom setup. Each built-in signal uses a benchmarked LLM prompt to classify traces and saves the results as comma-delimited tags representing the detected issues.

Signals use a [Serverless Inference](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/inference/serverless.md) model to score traces, so you don't need external API keys.

Weave provides 13 preset signals organized into two groups.

results.heading: Signals and custom monitors
results.snippet:
## Signals and custom monitors

Use [signals](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/evaluation/monitors.md), preset automated scorers for production traces, to get started with production monitoring quickly, then add custom monitors for evaluation criteria specific to your application.

| | Signals | Custom monitors |
| - | - | - |
| **Configuration** | One-click enable, no prompt writing | Full control over scoring prompt, model, and parameters |
| **Scope** | Preset quality and error classifiers | Any evaluation criteria you define |
| **Trace selection** | Automatic (successful root traces for quality, failed traces for errors) | Configurable operations, filters, and sampling rate |
| **Model** | Serverless Inference (preset) | Any commercial or Serverless Inference model |
| **Use case** | Quick production monitoring with proven classifiers | Custom evaluation criteria specific to your application |

### Trace

A *Trace* captures the full Call stack for a single operation. Threads group traces together that are part of the same logical conversation or session. In other words, a thread is made up of multiple turns, each representing one part in the conversation. For more information about Traces, see the [Tracing overview](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/tracking/tracing.md).

# Integrations overview

> Trace agents and LLM applications with Weave's integrations for agent SDKs, harnesses, LLM providers, and orchestration frameworks.

Weave provides two ways to integrate with your AI stack:

* **Trace agents**: for multi-turn agentic applications built with agent SDKs (such as the OpenAI Agents SDK or Google ADK) or run inside agent harnesses (such as Claude Code, Codex, or Pi.dev). These integrations capture sessions, turns, LLM calls, and tool calls, and render them in the Weave **Agents** view.
* **Trace LLM applications**: for code that calls LLM providers (OpenAI, Anthropic, Bedrock, and others) or uses orchestration frameworks (LangChain, LlamaIndex, DSPy, and others). These integrations capture individual LLM calls and pipeline steps as Weave **Calls** in the **Traces** view.

results.title: Koog
results.heading: What gets traced
results.snippet:
## What gets traced

After you run an agent with the exporter enabled, Koog forwards traces to your Weave project. Koog's Weave exporter captures the same spans as Koog's general OTEL integration, including:

* Agent lifecycle events (start, stop, errors)
* LLM interactions (prompts, completions, token usage, latency)
* Tool and API calls (function calls and external requests)
* System context (model name, Koog version, environment metadata)

You can visualize these traces in the Weights & Biases UI to understand performance and quality. See [Weave's tracing overview](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/tracking/tracing.md) for an introduction to capturing traces with Weave.

> Evaluate AI outputs and return evaluation metrics with Weave Scorers

In Weave, Scorers evaluate AI outputs and return evaluation metrics. They take the AI's output, analyze it, and return a dictionary of results. Scorers can use your input data as reference if needed and can also output extra information, such as explanations or reasoning from the evaluation.

# Evaluations overview

> Evaluation-driven LLM application development to systematically improve applications

*Evaluation-driven LLM application development* helps you systematically improve LLM applications by measuring their behavior using consistent, curated examples.

This guide shows you how to set up and run evaluations in Weave so you can measure your LLM application's performance against repeatable test cases, compare changes over time, and identify regressions. It's intended for developers building LLM applications who want to move beyond ad hoc testing into a structured, measurable workflow.

**Python**

In Weave, the core of the workflow is the *`Evaluation` object*, which defines:

* A [`Dataset`](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/core-types/datasets) or list of dictionaries for test examples.
* One or more [scoring functions](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/evaluation/scorers.md).
* Optional configuration like [input preprocessing](#format-dataset-rows-before-evaluating).

Once you've defined the `Evaluation`, you can run it against a [`Model`](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/core-types/models) object or any custom function containing LLM application logic. Each call to `.evaluate()` triggers an *evaluation run*. Think of the `Evaluation` object as a blueprint, and each run as a measurement of how your application performs under that setup.

**TypeScript**

In Weave, the core of the workflow is the *`Evaluation` object*, which defines:

* A [`Dataset`](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/core-types/datasets) or array of objects for test examples.
* One or more [scoring functions](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/evaluation/scorers.md).

Once you've defined the `Evaluation`, you can run it against any function wrapped with `weave.op`. Each call to `.evaluate()` triggers an *evaluation run*. Think of the `Evaluation` object as a blueprint, and each run as a measurement of how your application performs under that setup.

> [!NOTE]
>
> The TypeScript SDK uses function-based models and scorers. Class-based `Model` and `Scorer` types are not yet available in TypeScript.

To get started with evaluations, complete the following steps:

1. [Create an `Evaluation` object](#create-an-evaluation-object)
2. [Define a dataset of examples](#define-a-dataset-of-test-examples)
3. [Define scoring functions](#define-scoring-functions)
4. [Define a model or function to evaluate](#define-a-model-or-function-to-evaluate)
5. [Run the evaluation](#run-the-evaluation)

After completing these steps, you'll have a reusable evaluation configuration and an evaluation run whose results you can inspect in the Weights & Biases UI. For a complete evaluation code sample, see the [full evaluation code example](#full-evaluation-code-example). You can also learn more about [advanced evaluation features](#advanced-evaluation-usage) like [Saved views](#saved-views) and [Imperative evaluations](#imperative-evaluations-evaluationlogger).

**Tracing is the record of activity.**

- An `Evaluation` object bundles a dataset of test examples with one or more scoring functions. You run it against a `Model` or a function that holds your application logic [S3].
- Each `.evaluate()` call is an evaluation run, and you inspect the results in the W&B UI [S3].
- The goal is to compare changes over time and catch regressions using consistent examples [S3].

**Signals are scoring and tagging of real agent activity.**
- In the Agents view, the Signals tab shows tags and ratings for your agent's conversations [S1].
- Tags are labels such as "user-frustration" or "nsfw". A rating is a number from 0.0 to 1.0 [S4].
- Signals flag quality and safety problems, help you find patterns, and point you to the traces that need attention [S1].
- Signals can score agent turns with an LLM judge or with an HTTP endpoint that you host [S1].
- The docs say Agent Lens uses the same trace data as Weave, so traces you already send appear there [S1]. Signals therefore work from the activity you have traced.

**How they fit together**
1. Trace your application or agent, so its activity is captured.
2. Use evaluations during development to score a model or function against fixed test examples. This tells you whether a change helped.
3. Use Signals on the traced agent conversations to surface issues as real users interact with it.

result.text:
## How Weave normalizes scores

Before Weave stores a signal result, it normalizes the tags, ratings, and reasons that the scorer returned:

* Tags are lowercased. Characters other than `0-9`, `a-z`, `A-Z`, space, and `. , ; - & ! @ # $ % ?` are removed. Runs of whitespace, underscores, and dashes collapse into one dash.
* At most 10 tags are kept per result. Duplicate tags are dropped.
* Reasons have the same characters removed and are truncated to 256 characters.
* A tag longer than 36 characters, or a result with more than one rating, is rejected as a whole, and Weave writes no feedback for it.

These rules apply to every signal, whether an LLM judge or a [remote scorer](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/tracking/remote-scorer-signals.md) produced the result.

Learn how to instrument a multi-turn agentic application using the W\&B Weave SDK so that you can view, debug, and evaluate your agent's behavior. This guide is intended for developers who build or integrate agents and want structured visibility into conversations, turns, LLM calls, and tool executions.

The Weave SDK for Agents models the full lifecycle of a multi-turn agent conversation: the agent that owns many conversations, the conversation that groups turns together, each user-agent exchange (turn), the LLM calls within a turn, and the tool executions that an LLM triggers. Traces appear in the **Agents** tab of your Weave project. Each conversation shows a multi-turn timeline with nested tool calls, token usage, and feedback.

Weave is built on [OpenTelemetry (OTel)](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/concepts/), the open standard for distributed tracing. Every turn, LLM call, and tool call emits an OTel *span* (a structured record of one operation). Each span is tagged with [GenAI semantic-convention](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/semconv/gen-ai/) attributes like `gen_ai.agent.name` and `gen_ai.conversation.id`.

If you're tracing individual functions as Ops with the `@weave.op` decorator, see [Trace LLM applications](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/tracking/tracing.md) instead.

The Weave SDK for Agents models the full lifecycle of a multi-turn agent conversation: the agent that owns many conversations, the conversation that groups turns together, each user-agent exchange (turn), the LLM calls within a turn, and the tool executions that an LLM triggers. Traces appear in the **Agents** tab of your Weave project. Each conversation shows a multi-turn timeline with nested tool calls, token usage, and feedback.

Weave is built on [OpenTelemetry (OTel)](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/concepts/), the open standard for distributed tracing. Every turn, LLM call, and tool call emits an OTel *span* (a structured record of one operation). Each span is tagged with [GenAI semantic-convention](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/semconv/gen-ai/) attributes like `gen_ai.agent.name` and `gen_ai.conversation.id`.

If you're tracing individual functions as Ops with the `@weave.op` decorator, see [Trace LLM applications](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/tracking/tracing.md) instead.

# View agent activity

> Use Weave's Agents view to understand what your agent did, how much it cost, and exactly where things went right or wrong.

> [!TIP]
>
> **This workflow is also available in CoreWeave Agent Lens.** Agent Lens is the Forge experience built for tracing, monitoring, and analyzing AI agents, with automated insights into agent failures and user intents. It uses the same trace data as Weights & Biases Weave, so the traces you already send appear there with nothing to migrate.
> [See how to do this in Agent Lens](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/agent-lens/conversations/view-activity.md).

The Agents view gives you a turn-by-turn record of every conversation your agent had, along with token usage, tool invocations, and execution spans.

Agent applications are hard to debug because the interesting behavior happens between the user's request and the final response. The Agents view in Weave makes that middle layer visible. Every conversation your agent had is captured here, with the full message history, span-level execution detail, and token costs attached. You can see at a glance whether an agent completed its task, how many tool calls it made, and where time or budget was spent. For teams building and iterating on agents, this is the starting point for understanding behavior in production.

Tracing captures what your agent or application does. Signals attach tags and ratings to the agent activity that tracing captures. Evaluations are a separate, dataset-based way to measure an application. The docs I read describe each piece but do not give one combined statement of how all three fit, so the relationships below are my reading of them.

**Tracing is the record.**
- With the Weave SDK for agents, every turn, LLM call, and tool call emits an OpenTelemetry span, which is a structured record of one operation [S8].
- Traces appear in the **Agents** tab. Each conversation shows a multi-turn timeline with nested tool calls, token usage, and feedback [S8].

**Signals are scoring on top of that agent activity.**
- In the Agents view, the Signals tab shows tags and ratings for your agent's conversations [S1].
- A rating is a number from 0.0 to 1.0 assigned to a matching span. Tags are labels on matching spans, such as "user-frustration" or "nsfw" [S4].
- Signals surface quality and safety issues, find patterns, and highlight the traces that need attention [S1].
- Because the Signals tab sits in the Agents view and its tags and ratings attach to spans, tracing is what produces the spans that Signals label. This is an inference. I did not find a sentence that says so directly.

**Evaluations are the structured test.**
- An `Evaluation` combines a dataset of test examples with one or more scoring functions. You run it against a `Model` or a function that holds your application logic [S3].
- Each `.evaluate()` call is an evaluation run. The aim is to measure behavior against repeatable examples, compare changes over time, and identify regressions [S3].

**How they relate**
- Tracing makes the activity visible.
- Evaluations check a version of your application against curated examples you chose.
- Signals score and tag the agent conversations that were actually traced, so you can see where to look.
- Evaluations and Signals both score outputs, but they work on different inputs.

**Limits:** I did not find a passage that says evaluations produce traces or feed Signals. I also did not read the tracing pages on Threads or the agent data model section.
